title: More Voiceprint Development (and site flow rework)
body: Along with Accent, Pitch, and Note, the last major element was Timbre. Timbre is really unique for everyone, more-so than everything else actually, so I knew visually it really had to make it's mark. I split Timbre into three scales based on how people (online) usually categorize someone's Timbre and what could accurately be picked up by a mic and detected by the API. So although nasal levels differ per Timbre, that could not be included because it doesn't reliably pick up on a laptop mic. Included: Bright <-> Dark, Breathy <-> Clean, Raspy <-> Smooth. SInce I was working with scales, I had their visual impacts also work as a scale of two extremes. For example, a more raspy voice would have a rougher, spiker core, while a smoother voice will have a perfect, glossy surface. Look on the final site to see how the other Timbre scales show up. The website housing my project was very underbaked since I was focusing on other aspects. So, once I got most of the other elements added, I made some classic wireframes to figure out how a user would go through my site. Since I knew a lot of my users would access my site through their phone, I made sure that the mobile version of the site also worked perfectly and was just as accessible.

title: Voiceprint Development
body: Accent and Note/Pitch are very important so I focused on breaking those down first, then adding in other elements later. The main color of a person's core (the inner sphere) is decided by their average Note. Their highest and lowest pitch shade the top and bottom of their core. 5 groups of accents, 16 total accents. 16 unique shell shapes in 5 families. Americas: Variations of geodesic spheres. British Isles: Variations of donut rings. Asia: Variations of flower inspired spheres. Oceania: Variations of two wings wrapping around. Africa & South Atlantic: Variations of spirals. How I came up with and assigned these looks for different accents varies from my personal interpretation to random (many are pretty random due to time constraints). The splotches of colors (at the time were just the opposite color of the note) are the person's vowel points projected/mapped onto a sphere. I feathered them so they would meld better with the core.

title: 3js Experiments
body: With the visuals I started from scratch. I needed to examine the data of the voices I had already collected and figure out which elements were most striking and unique across the board. Something I needed to work on was making a proper hierarchy- giving the most visual weight to the most unique aspects of someone's voice such as Accent and Note/Pitch. I then spent a lot of time figuring out how to form individual's voice portraits or "Voiceprints" as I call them. I switched from 2D to 3D using 3js generated shapes because it gave the Voiceprints more dimension (literally), and I loved the idea of users being able to spin the visual around to explore it.

title: Starting Prototype 1
body: This week focused on finding the correct tools and APIs to use. Then, after understanding which elements of a voice I can measure, I needed to figure out how to visualize it. Originally, I wanted the final portrait for each person to be abstract and unique. I gave every single part of the voice I was turning into data similar visual weight. I was also using the visualization of the person speaking the entire sentence, showing changes over time. The result was rather muddy looking and unfocused- especially when looked at in a group. Since I spent most of my time making sure my site was functional, not too much thought was put into the visual elements at this time.
